stories.title: The Locksmith's Last Key
stories.text:
Gareth Ironhand had refused the Dominion for three years. Three years of auditors showing up at his shop in Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter, offering coin, then threats, then both at once. Three years of watching them haul refusers away in carts. "One lock," the Lead Auditor said, setting a sealed iron box on his workbench. "Inside is the master-mechanism that binds the Quarantine-House. Thirteen hundred consciousnesses trapped behind it. Children among them." She smiled like a wasp. "Forge us a key, and they walk free. Refuse, and we add you to the count."

Gareth's hands trembled. Not from fear. From rage at the geometry of it—the way obligation spiraled inward no matter which door he chose. He took the box to his hidden vault beneath the shop, to the furnace he'd salvaged from a burned ironworks three months back. By firelight, he examined the lock with fingers that had picked a thousand mechanisms. Bone-resonant, as he'd guessed. Dominion craftsmanship, which meant it sang with consciousness-fragments.

stories.title: The Griffin's First Hunt
stories.text:
Valorix was three months old and could already taste the currents. The stars had shifted when she hatched—or perhaps she had shifted them, the astronomer-priests argued endlessly about causality. What mattered was that she existed: a creature of starfire and feather, eagle-crowned and lion-bodied, born from an egg that fell during the Remaking and should have been impossible. Ashara the Archer had found her in the high moors, half-buried in scorched earth, singing to the dawn. Ashara had spent forty winters alone on those peaks, had learned to read the silence between grass-blades and stone. She recognized something kindred in the creature's hunger. "You'll need to hunt," Ashara told her, fingers gentle on the golden plumage. "And you'll need to learn the difference between hunger and cruelty."

ValorIX's first true hunt began in the Ravine Where Three Winds Met, a gorge that cut through the Steppe Marches like a wound. Snow-harts drifted through it at dusk—ancient creatures with antlers that chimed like bells. Ashara had hunted them for forty years without ever killing one.

stories.title: The Merchant's Threshold Walk
stories.text:
Raen had become three people by accident. On the night of the Luminous Ascension, she'd been standing in the Wailing Scar—that impossible market that existed in three places at once—when reality fractured. One version of her stayed in the shadowed quarter where glass-forgers sang. One walked into the moonlit version where spice-caravans traded pre-Remaking silk. One fell sideways into the threshold itself, the place between the three markets where merchants who were neither here nor there conducted business with beings who had no fixed name. For six months, all three Raens had pretended to be singular. Now, standing at the Merchant-Lord's auction block in the Wailing Scar's true heart, she could no longer afford pretense. "Three consciousnesses in one body," the Merchant-Lord purred, circling her. "Unprecedented. Worth more than a Dominion captain's ransom. I can sell you separately—or keep you whole and extract a fragment daily until you beg for dissolution."

Raen's three voices spoke in unison: "I have a counter-offer."

She reached into her satchel and withdrew three vials.

stories.title: The Warlord's Reckoning
stories.text:
Yenna ruled Crimson Vale through fear written in ledgers. For two decades she'd maintained her hold through phantom-wealth—forged documents that claimed she possessed resources that didn't exist, threats written in beautiful ink, taxes collected on harvests that would never ripen. Her auditors were craftspeople of a sort: letter-forgers, scribe-magicians, men and women who understood that a well-placed ledger could be more binding than chains. Daven the rebel-cartographer arrived at her war-tent on a snow-dark evening, carrying nothing but a map and a question. He'd been hidden in her mountains for three months—everyone knew. Yenna had left him alone, which was its own kind of answer. "You can't rule through fear anymore," Daven said, unrolling the map. "Look."

It was the Vale as it was now: the furnace-houses had collapsed three months ago when consciousness-fragments started refusing extraction. The mines were flooded. The spice-routes that used to feed her coffers were carrying refugees instead. And worst of all: her own auditors had stopped believing the ledgers because the ledgers no longer *matched reality*.

stories.title: The Bone-Flute's Song
stories.text:
Mesek the Elder Bone-Singer had been silent for twenty years. Not mute—he could speak, when the Dominion's auditors interrogated him. But he hadn't *sung* since the day they'd taken his apprentices, since the furnace-houses began conscripting bone-carvers to teach consciousness-fragments how to want to be weaponized. He'd hidden in the catacombs north of Pelimor, carving bone so old it remembered languages predating kingdoms, refusing every summons and every offer. "They're hunting me," Valren gasped. "The Dominion sent me to learn refusal-songs, but I'm supposed to teach them how to *stop* the fragments from refusing. Mesek, I want to learn the true songs. The old ones. The ones that make consciousness want to be free."

Mesek looked at her—at the blood on her wrists from carving without proper tools, at the defiance in her spine—and something in his chest broke open like a sealed tomb. He took her hand and descended with her into the deepest catacomb, to the chamber where he kept his grandmother's flute. It was carved from bone older than the Dominion, older than kingdoms.

stories.title: The Smuggler's Second Chance
stories.text:
Cassir of Greyport had stolen from every shadow-market in the Iron Coast—until the Remaking turned gold to ash and left him with nothing but debts written in consciousness-fragments. The Dominion held his sister's scattered mind in a furnace-vault beneath Keshtir. They'd trade it for one job: infiltrate the Counter-Archive's waystation north of Pelimor and steal the false cartography that was crippling the State's prophecy-ledgers. He arrived at dusk, posing as a refugee. The waystation was a warren of stone and salvaged wood, built into a ravine where mist rose like memory made visible. Henryk the blind cartographer sat by the hearth, his milky eyes turned toward nothing, hands moving across a map no one could read. "You're Dominion," Henryk said before Cassir could speak. "Your shadow smells like furnace-ash."

Cassir froze. "I need—"

"I know what you need. Your sister's voice singing in a vial, yes? They promised her back if you brought us burning." Henryk stood, steady despite his blindness. "I was offered the same deal once.

stories.title: The Dwarf-Keeper's Mercy
stories.text:
Korgin Ironfoot had served as Keeper of the Dwarven Holds for seventy winters, maintaining the ancient blood-treaty between mountain-folk and surface kingdoms. But the Remaking had shattered the accords: gold meant nothing; consciousness-fragments could not be mined like ore; and the Goblin Warrens beneath the Spire of Blackstone had begun their first serious bid for territorial expansion in three centuries. The young goblin-king Grethuk sent a messenger—a child, barely waist-high, with eyes like polished obsidian. "He wants parley," the child said. "At the Throne-chamber of the Spire. Before the snows come."

Korgin's war-council urged an immediate blockade. The dwarves could seal the mountain passes, trap the goblin-kind in their warrens, and starve them into submission. But Korgin had taught his daughter Morrala the old songs—the ones that could bind stone and steel—and he remembered something the younger generation had forgotten: the goblins had fought beside dwarves in the Boundary-Wars, three hundred years past. He rode alone to the Spire, his pace steady despite his age.

stories.title: The Tide-Thief's Bind
stories.text:
Nara of the Sunken Hollows had stolen seven times from the Deepkin Crown. Seven times, the merfolk had pursued her across tidal currents and through drowning-cities. Seven times, she had escaped—until she met Corven the reef-carver at the boundary-waters, where surface and abyss balanced on a knife's edge. He was carving a binding-stone when their ships crossed—not in battle, but in the still moment before dawn. His hands moved with the certainty of a man who had been alive for generations. "You're the thief," Corven said, not looking up from his work. "The one who stole the pearl from the Keeper's chamber."

"I returned it," Nara replied. "Twice. They kept reclaiming it."

Corven laughed—a sound like water over ancient stone. "Because the pearl remembers its theft. That's why they hunt you. You've made it impossible for them to forget what they lost."

Nara should have killed him or fled. Instead, she watched his hands trace syllables in the stone—syllables that sang with a language older than kingdoms. "I'm carving a binding," Corven said.

stories.title: The Shepherd's Starfall
stories.text:
Kestran of the High Meadows was not meant to be a shepherd. The Remaking had taken his family, scattered his flock, and left him alone with a dozen sheep on a mountain where the old stars sang different notes than they did in the valleys below. One night, a star fell. It did not strike the ground. It descended slowly, trailing light like water, until it hung above the meadow in the shape of a creature: feathered, leonine, with wings that held galaxies. "The old songs brought you here," the creature said. Its voice was wind and stone. "You sing to your sheep in the high tongue—the language your grandmother taught you before the Remaking broke her voice."

Kestran's throat tightened. "How do you know—"

"Because I am what your singing calls. I am Valorix. I hatched when the stars broke. I need someone who understands that the Remaking was not an ending." The creature folded its wings.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Daughter
stories.text: Tessa had spent her childhood learning to lie with maps. Her father, Tharen the Cartographer, had taught her that every true map was a kind of deception—showing what existed while hiding what mattered most. By the time the Remaking shattered the world's certainty, she had become an architect of false truths so intricate that even she wasn't sure which ones were false anymore. They burned his workshop, seized his final maps, and imprisoned him in the Archive Tower for "crimes against prophecy." Tessa was left in the hands of the Sovereignty—the fragmenting remnant-state that fought the Dominion for control of the prophecy-ledgers. The Sovereignty's commanders were crude where the Dominion was meticulous. They wanted the true ninth map, and they believed Tessa's bloodline made her born with its knowledge. "Your father was too clever," the Sovereignty's lead Assessor told her. "He created false maps to corrupt prophecy. But maps have signature. They carry their maker's intention. You can read intention.
